On converse invariant trees of diameter four

Fernando Afonso11 1 Instituto de Matemática e Estatística, Universidade de São Paulo, Brazil fernando.s.afonso@usp.br   Lucas Colucci22 2 Instituto de Matemática e Estatística, Universidade de São Paulo, Brazil tnaia@crm.cat, research supported by FAPESB (EDITAL FAPESB Nº 012/2022 - UNIVERSAL - NºAPP0044/2023). FAPESB is the Bahia Research Foundation.   Tássio Naia33 3 Centre de Recerca Matemàtica, Edifici C, Campus Bellaterra, 08193, Spain, tnaia@crm.cat, research supported by the European Union’s Horizon Europe Marie Skłodowska-Curie grant PARTIORI – project number 101207083 .

Abstract

Let DD be an oriented graph, and let fT​(D)f_{T}(D) denote the number of copies of DD in a tournament TT. We say that DD is converse invariant if fT​(D)=fT​(D¯)f_{T}(D)=f_{T}(\overline{D}) for every tournament TT, where D¯\overline{D} is obtained from DD by reversing all arcs. Ai, Gutin, Lei, Yeo, and Zhou introduced a digraph polynomial for studying this property and conjectured that an orientation of a tree of maximum degree at least 33 is converse invariant if and only if it is self-converse or can be obtained recursively by bridge-mirroring from an orientation of a path.

We disprove this conjecture. More precisely, we characterize converse-invariant orientations of trees of diameter four and exhibit non-self-converse examples that do not arise from the recursive bridge-mirroring construction. To prove the classification, we introduce a multilinear polynomial PDP_{D} encoding the difference fT​(D)−fT​(D¯)f_{T}(D)-f_{T}(\overline{D}) over all tournaments TT, and we give a coefficient formula for PDP_{D} as a signed sum over copies of subgraphs of the underlying graph of DD. This polynomial method yields parity obstructions, gives new proofs that oriented paths and cycles are converse invariant, and provides the main tool for the diameter-four classification.

1 Introduction

Let DD be an oriented graph, i.e., a simple digraph without loops and having no opposite pairs of directed edges, and TT be a tournament. We denote by fT​(D)f_{T}(D) the number of copies of DD in TT, i.e., the number of subdigraphs of TT isomorphic to DD, and by D¯\overline{D} the converse oriented graph of DD, i.e., the oriented graph obtained from DD by changing the direction of every arc of DD. In this paper, we are interested in studying oriented graphs DD that satisfy fT​(D)=fT¯​(D)f_{T}(D)=f_{\overline{T}}(D), or, equivalently, fT​(D)=fT​(D¯)f_{T}(D)=f_{T}({\overline{D}}), for every tournament TT. We say that the oriented graph is converse invariant if this condition holds.

An oriented graph DD is called self-converse if DD and D¯\overline{D} are isomorphic oriented graphs. Clearly, every self-converse oriented graph is converse invariant. In 2023, El Sahili and Hanna [2] asked whether it is possible to characterize the converse invariant digraphs, and found the first family of converse invariant digraphs that are not necessarily self-converse:

{theorem}

[ (El Sahili, Hanna) [2]] Every oriented path and cycle is converse invariant.

More recently, in 2025, Ai, Gutin, Lei, Yeo, and Zhou [1] classified converse invariant oriented trees of diameter at most 3:

{theorem}

[ (Ai, Gutin, Lei, Yeo, Zhou) [1]] Let DD be an orientation of a tree with diameter at most three that is not a path. Then DD is converse invariant if and only if it is self-converse, or DD or its converse is isomorphic to the digraph shown in Figure 1.

For a digraph DD and u∈V⁡(D)u\in V(D), the bridge-mirroring of DD at the vertex uu is the digraph obtained by taking two copies of DD and adding an arc between the two vertices corresponding to uu. This operation was introduced by Zhao and Zhou [3].

In [1], it was proved that the bridge-mirroring preserves the converse invariance property. Furthermore, the authors conjecture that this is essentially the only way to produce converse invariant trees:

{conjecture}

[ (Ai, Gutin, Lei, Yeo, Zhou) [1]] Let TT be an orientation of a tree with maximum degree at least 3. Then TT is converse invariant if and only if it is self-converse or TT can be obtained by the bridge-mirroring operation recursively from an orientation of a path.

In this paper, we disprove Conjecture 1, and introduce a new polynomial that encodes the orientations of a tournament that allow us to find new obstructions for a digraph to be converse invariant (Theorem 3), give new proofs of Theorems 1 and 1 and characterize the converse invariant diameter-four trees as follows:

{definition}

Let h⩾1h\geqslant 1. An oriented tree TT belongs to the family ℰ4\mathcal{E}_{4} if it is constructed as follows. Start with a path

x−u−yx-u-y

and attach 2​h2h leaves to each of the three vertices x,u,yx,u,y. Orient the 2​h2h pendant edges incident with each of x,u,yx,u,y so that exactly hh of them point away from the center and exactly hh point towards the center. Finally, orient the two edges x​uxu and u​yuy either both towards uu, or both away from uu.

Equivalently, TT is obtained from three copies of the same balanced oriented star by identifying their centers with the vertices of a path of length two, and orienting the two edges of this path so that the middle vertex is either a source or a sink.

Our main result, proved in Section 4.3, is the following classification of diameter-four converse invariant trees:

{theorem}

Let TT be an orientation of a tree of diameter four which is not a path. Then TT is converse invariant if and only if either TT is self-converse or T∈ℰ4T\in\mathcal{E}_{4}.

2 Preliminaries

It is enough to test converse invariance on tournaments with exactly |V⁡(D)||V(D)| vertices. Indeed, if the equality holds for every tournament on |V⁡(D)||V(D)| vertices and TT is a larger tournament, then summing the equality over all |V⁡(D)||V(D)|-vertex subtournaments of TT gives fT​(D)=fT​(D¯)f_{T}(D)=f_{T}(\overline{D}), since each copy of DD uses exactly |V⁡(D)||V(D)| vertices. Throughout the paper, UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) denotes the underlying graph of DD, obtained from DD by ignoring the orientations of the edges.

Let DD be an oriented graph on nn vertices and put e⁡(D)=|E⁡(D)|e(D)=|E(D)|. We shall associate to DD a multilinear polynomial PDP_{D} whose non-vanishing on a point of {±1}(n2)\{\pm 1\}^{\binom{n}{2}} is equivalent to the existence of a tournament TT with fT​(D)≠fT​(D¯)f_{T}(D)\neq f_{T}(\overline{D}).

Index the vertices of both DD and a tournament TT by [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}. For each unordered pair i​jij, let xi​j=xj​ix_{ij}=x_{ji} be 11 if the edge of TT is directed from min⁡(i,j)\min(i,j) to max⁡(i,j)\max(i,j), and −1-1 otherwise. Similarly, for each edge i​j∈E⁡(D)ij\in E(D), let yi​j=yj​iy_{ij}=y_{ji} be 11 if the arc of DD is directed from min⁡(i,j)\min(i,j) to max⁡(i,j)\max(i,j), and −1-1 otherwise. When DD is acyclic, we shall always choose a topological labeling of DD, so that yi​j=1y_{ij}=1 for every edge i​j∈E⁡(D)ij\in E(D).

For a permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n}, we embed vertex ii of DD into vertex π⁡(i)\pi(i) of TT. This embedding is a copy of DD if and only if

xπ⁡(i)​π​(j)​yi​j​(−1)(i​j)π=1x_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}y_{ij}(-1)^{(ij)_{\pi}}=1

fT​(D)=1|Aut​(D)|​∑π∈Sn∏i​j∈E⁡(D)1+xπ⁡(i)​π​(j)​yi​j​(−1)(i​j)π2.f_{T}(D)=\frac{1}{|\text{Aut}(D)|}\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\prod_{ij\in E(D)}\frac{1+x_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}y_{ij}(-1)^{(ij)_{\pi}}}{2}.

=∑π∈Sn(∏i​j∈E⁡(D)(1+xπ⁡(i)​π​(j)​yi​j​(−1)(i​j)π)−∏i​j∈E⁡(D)(1−xπ⁡(i)​π​(j)​yi​j​(−1)(i​j)π)).\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in S_{n}}\left(\prod_{ij\in E(D)}\bigl(1+x_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}y_{ij}(-1)^{(ij)_{\pi}}\bigr)-\prod_{ij\in E(D)}\bigl(1-x_{\pi(i)\pi(j)}y_{ij}(-1)^{(ij)_{\pi}}\bigr)\right).

Hence, an oriented graph DD is converse invariant if, and only if, every coefficient of PDP_{D} is zero.

3 First results

In this section we prove two consequences of the coefficient formula. The first is a parity obstruction to converse invariance. The second is a polynomial proof of Theorem 1.

{theorem}

Let DD be an oriented graph with underlying graph GG. Suppose that GG has a subgraph HH such that

  1. 1.

    HH has an odd number of edges;

  2. 2.

    |Aut​(H)||\text{Aut}(H)| is odd;

  3. 3.

    the number of copies of HH in GG is odd.

Then DD is not converse invariant. In particular, if GG has an odd number of edges and |Aut​(G)||\text{Aut}(G)| is odd, then DD is not converse invariant.

Proof.

Let H′⊆KnH^{\prime}\subseteq K_{n} be any labeled copy of HH, with each edge oriented from the smaller label to the larger label. By (1), the coefficient of xH′x^{H^{\prime}} in PDP_{D} is

2​(n−|V⁡(H′)|)!​∑S∑α∏i​j∈E⁡(S)yi​j​(−1)(i​j)α,2(n-|V(H^{\prime})|)!\sum_{S}\sum_{\alpha}\prod_{ij\in E(S)}y_{ij}(-1)^{(ij)_{\alpha}},

where SS ranges over the copies of HH in GG and α:S→H′\alpha:S\to H^{\prime} ranges over graph isomorphisms. Each summand is +1+1 or −1-1. The number of summands is

#​{copies of ​H​ in ​G}⋅|Aut​(H)|,\#\{\text{copies of }H\text{ in }G\}\cdot|\text{Aut}(H)|,

which is odd by assumption. A sum of an odd number of signs cannot be zero, so this coefficient is nonzero. Hence PDP_{D} is not the zero polynomial, and DD is not converse invariant. ∎

{theorem}

Oriented paths and oriented cycles are converse invariant.

Proof.

By the coefficient criterion, it is enough to prove that every coefficient (1) is zero. We first consider the case where DD is an oriented path. Since DD is acyclic, we take a topological labeling and hence yi​j=1y_{ij}=1 for every i​j∈E⁡(D)ij\in E(D).

Let HH be a subgraph of UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) with an odd number of edges. Then HH is a disjoint union of paths, and at least one component, say QQ, has an odd number of edges. Let ρ\rho be the automorphism of HH that reflects QQ and fixes every vertex outside QQ. For every copy SS of HH in UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) and every isomorphism α:S→H\alpha:S\to H, pair α\alpha with ρ∘α\rho\circ\alpha. This pairing has no fixed point.

We claim that the two paired isomorphisms contribute opposite signs to (1). Outside the component α−1​(Q)\alpha^{-1}(Q), the two products are identical. On QQ, write the vertices in path order as v1,…,v2​rv_{1},\dots,v_{2r}, so that QQ has 2​r−12r-1 edges. The reflection pairs all edges except the middle edge vr​vr+1v_{r}v_{r+1}; the paired edges contribute the same product before and after applying the reflection, while the middle edge is reversed. Thus

∏i​j∈E⁡(S)(−1)(i​j)α=−∏i​j∈E⁡(S)(−1)(i​j)ρ∘α.\prod_{ij\in E(S)}(-1)^{(ij)_{\alpha}}=-\prod_{ij\in E(S)}(-1)^{(ij)_{\rho\circ\alpha}}.

Hence the contributions cancel in pairs, and every coefficient is zero.

The proof for cycles is the same, except for one case. If HH is a proper subgraph of a cycle, then HH is a disjoint union of paths, so the preceding argument applies to a path component with an odd number of edges. If HH is the whole cycle, then |E⁡(H)||E(H)| must be odd. Pair each isomorphism with a reflection of the odd cycle whose axis passes through one vertex and the midpoint of the opposite edge. This reflection fixes exactly one edge setwise and reverses its endpoints, while all other edges are paired. Therefore the sign changes by a factor of −1-1, and the contributions again cancel. The factor ∏i​j∈E⁡(S)yi​j\prod_{ij\in E(S)}y_{ij} is independent of α\alpha, so the argument applies to every orientation of the cycle. ∎

4 Trees

In this section, we will deal with theorems concerning trees. As they do not contain cycles, every orientation of a tree corresponds to a labeling and vice versa in the natural way, i.e., the edges point towards the larger label.

4.1 Lemmas

In this subsection, we will prove some relevant lemmas that will be used in subsections 4.2 and 4.3. We start with a definition:

{definition}

Let SS and TT be two labeled isomorphic graphs, and α:V⁡(S)→V⁡(T)\alpha:V(S)\rightarrow V(T) be an isomorphism. We define the sign of α\alpha along the edges of SS as

sgnS​(α)=∏i​j∈E⁡(S)(−1)(i​j)α.\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha)=\prod_{ij\in E(S)}(-1)^{(ij)_{\alpha}}.
{lemma}

Let SS and TT be labeled stars with |V⁡(S)|=|V⁡(T)|⩾3|V(S)|=|V(T)|\geqslant 3. Then sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) is the same for every isomorphism α:S→T\alpha:S\to T.

Proof.

Any two isomorphisms S→TS\to T differ by a permutation of the leaves of SS. Since such permutations are generated by transpositions, it is enough to compare α\alpha with the map obtained from α\alpha by swapping the images of two leaves.

Let cc be the label of the center of TT, and let p<qp<q be the two leaf-images being swapped. All factors in sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) are unchanged except possibly those corresponding to the two leaf-edges whose images are incident with pp and qq. If pp and qq lie on the same side of cc, neither of these two factors changes. If p<c<qp<c<q, then both factors change sign. In both cases their product is unchanged. Hence sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) is independent of α\alpha. ∎

{definition}

A rooted tree TT is a tree with a distinguished vertex r∈V⁡(T)r\in V(T), called the root. A rooted isomorphism between rooted trees is an isomorphism that maps the root of the first tree to the root of the second. For a vertex xx in a rooted tree, R⁡(x)R(x) denotes the subtree induced by xx and its descendants. Finally, ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} denotes the orientation of the rooted tree TT in which every edge points away from the root.

{lemma}

Let SS and TT be isomorphic rooted labeled trees. Then sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) is the same for every rooted isomorphism α:S→T\alpha:S\to T. In particular, if SS and TT are isomorphic trees of even diameter, then sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) is the same for every isomorphism α:S→T\alpha:S\to T.

Proof.

We prove the first statement by induction on |V⁡(S)||V(S)|. The cases of one edge and of rooted stars follow from the definition and Lemma 4.1.

Let rSr_{S} and rTr_{T} be the roots. The children of rSr_{S} split into classes according to the rooted isomorphism type of the subtrees below them; the same is true for rTr_{T}. A rooted isomorphism is obtained by, independently for each class, matching the corresponding child-subtrees of rSr_{S} with those of rTr_{T}, and then choosing rooted isomorphisms inside the matched subtrees.

By the induction hypothesis, the contribution from the edges inside each matched child-subtree is independent of the chosen rooted isomorphism inside that subtree. It remains to check that permuting isomorphic child-subtrees within one class does not change the contribution of the edges incident with the parent. But these parent–child edges form a star, and Lemma 4.1 shows that their contribution is invariant under such permutations. Therefore the full product defining sgnS​(α)\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha) is independent of α\alpha.

If a tree has even diameter, then it has a unique central vertex. Every isomorphism between two such trees maps the center to the center, and hence is a rooted isomorphism after rooting both trees at their centers. This proves the second statement. ∎

{corollary}

Let SS be a rooted oriented tree, with a labeling induced by its orientation. Then

sgnS​(α)=(−1)r\text{sgn}_{S}(\alpha)=(-1)^{r}

for every rooted isomorphism α:S→Sout\alpha:S\to S_{\mathrm{out}}, where rr is the number of edges of SS directed towards the root. In particular, if S1S_{1} and S2S_{2} are isomorphic rooted oriented trees and α:S1→Sout\alpha:S_{1}\to S_{\mathrm{out}}, β:S2→Sout\beta:S_{2}\to S_{\mathrm{out}} are rooted isomorphisms, then sgnS1​(α)=sgnS2​(β)\text{sgn}_{S_{1}}(\alpha)=\text{sgn}_{S_{2}}(\beta) if the corresponding numbers of inward edges have the same parity, and the two signs are opposite otherwise.

Proof.

Consider first one rooted isomorphism α:S→Sout\alpha:S\to S_{\mathrm{out}}. Since the labels of both trees are induced by their orientations, an edge contributes −1-1 precisely when its direction in SS is opposite to its direction in SoutS_{\mathrm{out}}, i.e., precisely when it is directed towards the root. Thus the product is (−1)r(-1)^{r}. Lemma 4.1 shows that the value does not depend on the chosen rooted isomorphism. The final assertion follows by applying this formula to S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}. ∎

4.2 Trees of diameter at most 33

In this subsection, we consider trees of diameter two and three. In particular, we give another proof of Theorem 1.

{proposition}

A star is converse invariant if and only if it is self-converse or a path.

Proof.

The path case follows from Theorem 3. Let DD be an orientation of a star that is not a path, let uu be its center, and let aa and bb be the indegree and outdegree of uu, respectively. Thus a+b⩾3a+b\geqslant 3.

First suppose that a+ba+b is odd. Then DD has an odd number of edges. For the monomial xDx^{D}, formula (1) gives

cD=2​∑α∈Aut​(D)sgnD​(α).c_{D}=2\sum_{\alpha\in\text{Aut}(D)}\text{sgn}_{D}(\alpha).

By Lemma 4.1, all terms in this sum have the same sign, so cD≠0c_{D}\neq 0. Hence a converse invariant star must have a+ba+b even.

Now assume a+ba+b is even. If necessary, replace DD by its converse, so that b>0b>0. Let HH be the star obtained from DD by deleting one out-edge of the center. The copies of HH in UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) are obtained by deleting one leaf-edge of DD. For each fixed copy, Lemma 4.1 makes the inner signed sum constant. Comparing with the identity embedding shows that deleting an in-edge and deleting an out-edge contribute opposite signs. Consequently cHc_{H} is a nonzero constant multiple of a−ba-b. Since DD is converse invariant, cH=0c_{H}=0, and therefore a=ba=b. This is exactly the condition that the oriented star be self-converse. ∎

We now give a polynomial proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1.

By Proposition 4.2, it remains to consider orientations of double stars. Let uu and vv be the two non-leaf vertices and orient the central edge as u→vu\to v. Let aa and bb be the numbers of in-leaves and out-leaves at uu, respectively, and let dd and cc be the numbers of in-leaves and out-leaves at vv, respectively. Put p=a+bp=a+b and q=c+dq=c+d.

We first show that p=qp=q. Suppose p≠qp\neq q. If p+qp+q is odd, let HH be the forest obtained from DD by deleting the central edge u​vuv. Then HH has an odd number of edges, and, because the two components have different sizes, it has a unique copy in UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D). The signed automorphism sum is nonzero by Lemma 4.1 applied to the two star components, so cH≠0c_{H}\neq 0. If p+qp+q is even, then DD has an odd number of edges. Since the two inner vertices have different degrees, every automorphism fixes them, and the same constant-sign argument gives cD≠0c_{D}\neq 0. In either case DD is not converse invariant, a contradiction. Hence p=qp=q.

If p=1p=1, the underlying tree is a path, which is excluded. Assume first that p⩾3p\geqslant 3. After possibly replacing DD by its converse and swapping the names of uu and vv, we may suppose that a>0a>0. Let HH be obtained from DD by deleting the central edge and one in-edge incident with uu. The copies of HH in UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) are obtained by deleting the central edge and one arbitrary leaf-edge. Since p⩾3p\geqslant 3, the two components of HH are stars of distinct sizes at least 22, and Lemma 4.1 makes each inner automorphism sum constant. A direct comparison with the identity embedding gives

cH=C⁡(a−b−c+d)c_{H}=C(a-b-c+d)

for some nonzero constant CC depending only on pp and on the labels. Since cH=0c_{H}=0 and a+b=c+da+b=c+d, we obtain a=ca=c and b=db=d. Thus DD is self-converse.

It remains to handle p=2p=2. Up to taking the converse and interchanging uu and vv, the double stars with two leaves at each inner vertex are either self-converse, the exceptional bridge-mirrored tree in Figure 1, or the case

(a,b,c,d)=(2,0,1,1).(a,b,c,d)=(2,0,1,1).

In this last case, let HH be the oriented star obtained by deleting from DD the two leaf-edges incident with vv. The only copies of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) in UG​(D)\textrm{UG}(D) are the stars centered at uu and at vv. For both copies, the signed automorphism sum has the same sign by Lemma 4.1 (equivalently, by Corollary 4.1, the two stars have the same parity of inward edges). Hence cH≠0c_{H}\neq 0, so this remaining case is not converse invariant. Therefore the only converse invariant double stars are the self-converse ones and the exceptional bridge-mirrored tree. ∎

4.3 Trees of diameter 44

In this subsection, TT will denote a converse invariant oriented tree of diameter four, with central vertex uu. We first prove a parity lemma valid for all such trees. We then prove the classification (Theorem 1) in two parts, according to whether uu has at least four non-leaf neighbors.

Let StS_{t} (t⩾0t\geqslant 0) denote the set of neighbors of uu with degree exactly t+1t+1 (i.e. that have tt children leaves), and TtT_{t} denote the subtree of TT induced by uu, StS_{t} and the leaves connected to the vertices of StS_{t}. For 0⩽l⩽t0\leqslant l\leqslant t, denote by AltA_{l}^{t} the set of out-neighbors of uu in StS_{t} with exactly ll leaves pointing towards them, and alt=|Alt|a_{l}^{t}=|A_{l}^{t}|. Symmetrically, let BltB_{l}^{t} denote the set of in-neighbors of uu in StS_{t} with exactly ll leaves pointing from them, and blt=|Blt|b_{l}^{t}=|B_{l}^{t}|. In particular, TtT_{t} being self-converse is equivalent to alt=blta_{l}^{t}=b_{l}^{t} for every l∈{0,…,t}l\in\{0,\dots,t\}, and TT is self-converse if and only if this condition holds for every tt.

We write

p⁡(T)=∑t⩾1|St|.p(T)=\sum_{t\geqslant 1}|S_{t}|.

Thus p⁡(T)p(T) is the number of neighbors of the central vertex which are not leaves.

{lemma}

Let TT be a converse invariant orientation of a tree of diameter four, with center uu. Then |St||S_{t}| is even for every t⩾0t\geqslant 0. In particular, TT has an even number of edges.

Proof.

First we prove that TT has an even number of edges. Suppose, to the contrary, that |E⁡(T)||E(T)| is odd. Since UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) has diameter four, it has the unique center uu. Hence every automorphism of UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) fixes uu. By Lemma 4.1, the quantity sgnT​(α)\text{sgn}_{T}(\alpha) is the same for every automorphism α\alpha of UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T). Therefore the coefficient of the monomial xTx^{T} is

cT=2​∑α∈Aut​(UG​(T))sgnT​(α),c_{T}=2\sum_{\alpha\in\text{Aut}(\textrm{UG}(T))}\text{sgn}_{T}(\alpha),

which is non-zero. This contradicts the converse invariance of TT. Thus |E⁡(T)||E(T)| is even.

We shall use the following simple rooted-profile observation. Suppose that a copy of a connected subgraph of UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) is rooted at uu. Its rooted branch profile records, for each s⩾0s\geqslant 0, the number of neighbors of uu which have exactly ss leaf-neighbors inside the copy. If one deletes a branch in S0S_{0}, then this profile changes only by decreasing the number of 00-branches by one. If one deletes one leaf-edge from a branch in SsS_{s}, with s⩾1s\geqslant 1, and ignores the isolated leaf, then the profile changes by decreasing the number of ss-branches by one and increasing the number of (s−1)(s-1)-branches by one. Finally, if one deletes the central edge of a branch in SsS_{s}, then one creates a detached star K1,sK_{1,s}. These effects are distinct and will be used below.

We start with t=0t=0. Suppose first that S0≠∅S_{0}\neq\varnothing. Let HH be the graph obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting one edge from uu to a vertex of S0S_{0}, ignoring the isolated vertex. Since deleting such an edge does not change the positive branches, the component of HH containing uu still has diameter four. Therefore every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) is rooted at the original center uu.

The rooted branch profile of HH has one fewer 00-branch than TT and the same number of ss-branches for every s⩾1s\geqslant 1. By the rooted-profile observation above, the only way to obtain this profile is to delete one branch in S0S_{0}. Hence every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) is obtained by deleting an edge from uu to a vertex of S0S_{0}.

For a fixed copy, Lemma 4.1 shows that the inner sum over isomorphisms is a non-zero constant. Moreover, deleting an edge directed away from uu gives the opposite sign from deleting an edge directed towards uu. Hence

cH=C⁡(a00−b00)c_{H}=C(a_{0}^{0}-b_{0}^{0})

for some non-zero constant CC. Since TT is converse invariant, we have cH=0c_{H}=0, and therefore a00=b00a_{0}^{0}=b_{0}^{0}. Thus

|S0|=a00+b00|S_{0}|=a_{0}^{0}+b_{0}^{0}

is even. If S0=∅S_{0}=\varnothing, this conclusion is trivial.

It remains to prove that |St||S_{t}| is even when t⩾1t\geqslant 1. Since UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) has diameter four, we have p⁡(T)⩾2p(T)\geqslant 2. We first prove the result when p⁡(T)⩾3p(T)\geqslant 3.

Suppose that S1≠∅S_{1}\neq\varnothing. Let HH be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting the unique leaf-edge incident with one vertex of S1S_{1}, again ignoring the isolated leaf. Since p⁡(T)⩾3p(T)\geqslant 3, the component containing uu still has at least two positive branches, and so has diameter four. Thus every copy is rooted at uu.

The rooted branch profile of HH is obtained from that of TT by replacing one 11-branch by one 00-branch. By the rooted-profile observation above, this can only come from deleting the unique leaf-edge of a branch in S1S_{1}. Therefore every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) is obtained by shortening one branch of S1S_{1} to a branch of S0S_{0}.

For a fixed copy, the inner isomorphism sum is again a non-zero constant. The sign of the deleted leaf-edge is +1+1 or −1-1 according to whether that leaf-edge is directed away from or towards the vertex of S1S_{1}. Consequently cHc_{H} is a signed sum of |S1||S_{1}| signs, all with the same non-zero multiplicative constant. If |S1||S_{1}| were odd, this signed sum could not be zero. Since cH=0c_{H}=0, we conclude that |S1||S_{1}| is even. If S1=∅S_{1}=\varnothing, this is trivial.

Now suppose that t⩾2t\geqslant 2. If St=∅S_{t}=\varnothing, there is nothing to prove. Let HH be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting the central edge u​vuv for one vertex v∈Stv\in S_{t}, while keeping all leaf-edges incident with vv. Then HH has no isolated vertices and has |V⁡(T)||V(T)| vertices and |E⁡(T)|−1|E(T)|-1 edges. Hence every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) is obtained from UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) by deleting exactly one edge.

The deleted edge cannot be a leaf-edge, since that would create an isolated vertex. It must therefore be a central edge. Moreover, deleting the central edge of a branch in SsS_{s} leaves a detached star K1,sK_{1,s}. Thus, in order to obtain a copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H), we must have s=ts=t. Hence the copies of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) are precisely the graphs obtained by deleting the central edge of one branch in StS_{t}.

Since p⁡(T)⩾3p(T)\geqslant 3, after deleting one positive branch the component containing uu still has at least two positive branches, and therefore has diameter four. Thus this component is rooted at uu. The other component is a star K1,tK_{1,t}. By Lemma 4.1 and Lemma 4.1, the inner isomorphism sum for each copy is a non-zero constant. Deleting a central edge oriented away from uu gives the opposite sign from deleting a central edge oriented towards uu. Hence cHc_{H} is a signed sum of |St||S_{t}| signs, all with the same non-zero multiplicative constant. If |St||S_{t}| were odd, then cH≠0c_{H}\neq 0, contradicting converse invariance. Therefore |St||S_{t}| is even.

This proves the lemma when p⁡(T)⩾3p(T)\geqslant 3.

Finally, let us consider the case p⁡(T)=2p(T)=2. Let xx and yy be the two non-leaf neighbors of uu. Suppose that xx has rr leaf-neighbors and yy has ss leaf-neighbors, with 1⩽r⩽s1\leqslant r\leqslant s, and m=|S0|m=|S_{0}|.

We now prove that r=sr=s. Suppose, for a contradiction, that r<sr<s. Since |E⁡(T)||E(T)| is even and mm is even, the number r+sr+s is even.

First assume that m≠rm\neq r. Let HH be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting the central edge u​yuy of the larger branch. Then HH has two components: a detached star K1,sK_{1,s}, and the component RR containing uu, which consists of the branch at xx together with the mm leaves adjacent to uu.

If m=0m=0, then RR is a star K1,r+1K_{1,r+1}. Since r+sr+s is even, we cannot have s=r+1s=r+1, and hence the two components of HH are not isomorphic. If m>0m>0, then RR has diameter three, whereas K1,sK_{1,s} has diameter two, so again the two components are not isomorphic.

Every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) has all vertices of TT and one edge less than TT. Thus it is obtained by deleting one edge of UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T). A leaf-edge deletion or an S0S_{0}-edge deletion would create an isolated vertex, which HH does not have. Hence the deleted edge must be one of u​xux and u​yuy. Deleting u​yuy gives the graph HH. Deleting u​xux gives a detached star K1,rK_{1,r} and the component consisting of the branch at yy together with the mm leaves adjacent to uu, which is not isomorphic to HH because r<sr<s and the component types described above do not match. Therefore every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) is obtained by deleting u​yuy.

For this unique type of copy, the inner isomorphism sum is non-zero. If m=0m=0, both components are non-isomorphic stars, and this follows from Lemma 4.1. If m>0m>0, the component RR has two non-leaf vertices of degrees m+1m+1 and r+1r+1, which are distinct because m≠rm\neq r; hence every automorphism of RR fixes these two vertices and only permutes leaves, so the signed automorphism sum is again non-zero. Thus cH≠0c_{H}\neq 0, contradicting converse invariance.

We may therefore assume that m=rm=r. Since mm is even, this gives r⩾2r\geqslant 2. Now let HH be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting the central edge u​xux of the smaller branch. The detached component is the star K1,rK_{1,r}, which is not a single edge. The component containing uu consists of the branch at yy together with the m=rm=r leaves adjacent to uu. As before, every copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) must be obtained by deleting one of the two central edges u​xux or u​yuy. Deleting u​xux gives HH. Deleting u​yuy gives a detached star K1,sK_{1,s} and a component whose two non-leaf vertices both have degree r+1r+1, and this is not isomorphic to HH. Therefore there is only one type of copy of UG​(H)\textrm{UG}(H) in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T).

The inner isomorphism sum is non-zero: the detached component is a star with at least three vertices, and the other component has two non-leaf vertices of distinct degrees, so its automorphisms only permute leaves. Consequently cH≠0c_{H}\neq 0, again contradicting converse invariance.

This contradiction proves that r=sr=s. Therefore the two positive branches both lie in the same set SrS_{r}, so |Sr|=2|S_{r}|=2, while every other StS_{t} with t⩾1t\geqslant 1 is empty. We have already proved that |S0||S_{0}| is even. Hence |St||S_{t}| is even for every t⩾0t\geqslant 0 in the case p⁡(T)=2p(T)=2 as well.

Combining the cases p⁡(T)⩾3p(T)\geqslant 3 and p⁡(T)=2p(T)=2 proves the lemma. ∎

We now begin to show Theorem 1 in the case p⁡(T)⩾4p(T)\geqslant 4. In this case we prove that TT is self-converse by showing inductively that each TtT_{t} is self-converse. We shall use the following polynomials: for 0⩽r⩽t0\leqslant r\leqslant t, put

Kr(t)​(x)=∑q=0r(−1)q​(xq)​(t−xr−q).K_{r}^{(t)}(x)=\sum_{q=0}^{r}(-1)^{q}\binom{x}{q}\binom{t-x}{r-q}.

{lemma}

Let w∈Ssw\in S_{s}.

  1. (i)

    Suppose that the edge u​wuw is kept and exactly rr leaf-edges incident with ww are deleted. Then the signed sum over all choices of these rr deleted leaf-edges is

    Kr(s)​(k)K_{r}^{(s)}(k)

    if w∈Aksw\in A_{k}^{s}, and

    (−1)r​Kr(s)​(k)(-1)^{r}K_{r}^{(s)}(k)

    if w∈Bksw\in B_{k}^{s}.

    Suppose that the edge u​wuw is deleted and all leaf-edges incident with ww are kept. Then the corresponding factor is

    η⁡(w)={+1,w∈Aks,−1,w∈Bks.\eta(w)=\begin{cases}+1,&w\in A_{k}^{s},\\ -1,&w\in B_{k}^{s}.\end{cases}
  3. (iii)

    If s=1s=1 and the whole branch at ww is deleted, then the corresponding factor is K1(1)​(k)K_{1}^{(1)}(k) both for w∈Ak1w\in A_{k}^{1} and for w∈Bk1w\in B_{k}^{1}.

Proof.

Suppose first that w∈Aksw\in A_{k}^{s}. Then u→wu\to w, and exactly kk leaf-edges point towards ww. If rr leaf-edges are deleted and exactly qq of them are among these kk inward leaf-edges, then the sign changes by (−1)q(-1)^{q}. Summing over qq gives

∑q=0r(−1)q​(kq)​(s−kr−q)=Kr(s)​(k).\sum_{q=0}^{r}(-1)^{q}\binom{k}{q}\binom{s-k}{r-q}=K_{r}^{(s)}(k).

Now suppose that w∈Bksw\in B_{k}^{s}. Then w→uw\to u, and exactly kk leaf-edges point away from ww, so s−ks-k leaf-edges point towards ww. Deleting rr leaf-edges gives the leaf contribution

∑q=0r(−1)q​(s−kq)​(kr−q)=(−1)r​Kr(s)​(k).\sum_{q=0}^{r}(-1)^{q}\binom{s-k}{q}\binom{k}{r-q}=(-1)^{r}K_{r}^{(s)}(k).

Since the central edge is kept in both the original branch and the selected sub-branch, the central sign cancels in the ratio. This proves (i).

If the central edge is deleted and all leaves are kept, then the leaf contribution is unchanged, and only the sign of the central edge is removed. This gives +1+1 in the AA-case and −1-1 in the BB-case, proving (ii).

Finally, assume s=1s=1 and the whole branch is deleted. The selected contribution is 11, so the ratio is the sign of the whole branch. In both the Ak1A_{k}^{1}-case and the Bk1B_{k}^{1}-case this sign is (−1)k=K1(1)​(k)(-1)^{k}=K_{1}^{(1)}(k). This proves (iii). ∎

{definition}

Assume that the relevant set StS_{t} is non-empty.

  1. (i)

    For t=0t=0 or t⩾2t\geqslant 2, let ZtZ^{t} be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting the central edge u​vuv for one vertex v∈Stv\in S_{t}, keeping all leaf-edges incident with vv if t⩾2t\geqslant 2.

    For t⩾1t\geqslant 1 and ll odd, 1⩽l⩽t1\leqslant l\leqslant t, let PltP_{l}^{t} be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by deleting ll leaf-edges incident with one vertex v∈Stv\in S_{t}, while keeping the central edge u​vuv.

    For t⩾2t\geqslant 2 and l⩾2l\geqslant 2 even, l⩽tl\leqslant t, let QltQ_{l}^{t} be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by choosing two distinct vertices a,v∈Sta,v\in S_{t}, deleting the central edge u​aua, keeping all leaf-edges incident with aa, and deleting ll leaf-edges incident with vv, while keeping u​vuv.

    If S1≠∅S_{1}\neq\varnothing, let Y1Y^{1} be obtained from ToutT_{\mathrm{out}} by choosing two distinct vertices a,v∈S1a,v\in S_{1}, deleting the whole branch at aa, and deleting the unique leaf-edge incident with vv.

The two distinct vertices required in the definitions of QltQ_{l}^{t} and Y1Y^{1} exist by Lemma 4.3. Moreover, all the graphs in Definition 4.3 have an odd number of edges, since TT has an even number of edges and in each case we delete an odd number of edges.

{lemma}

Assume that p⁡(T)⩾4p(T)\geqslant 4. For every graph in Definition 4.3, every copy of its underlying graph in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) sends the component of diameter four to a subgraph centered at the original center uu of TT. Consequently, every such copy may be treated as a rooted copy with root uu in the coefficient formula. Moreover, none of these graphs has a connected component consisting of a single edge.

Proof.

The graph PltP_{l}^{t} is connected. It is obtained by shortening at most one positive branch, so it still contains at least p⁡(T)−1⩾3p(T)-1\geqslant 3 positive branches. Hence it contains a path of length four, and has diameter four.

For ZtZ^{t} with t⩾2t\geqslant 2, the graph has one detached star K1,tK_{1,t} and one component containing uu. The component containing uu has at least p⁡(T)−1⩾3p(T)-1\geqslant 3 positive branches, and hence has diameter four. The detached component has diameter two. For Z0Z^{0}, the graph is connected and still contains all positive branches, so it has diameter four.

For QltQ_{l}^{t}, the component containing uu loses the anchor branch, and the probe branch may be shortened all the way to a leaf-branch. Nevertheless it still contains at least p⁡(T)−2⩾2p(T)-2\geqslant 2 positive branches, and hence has diameter four. The detached component is a star K1,tK_{1,t} with t⩾2t\geqslant 2. The same argument applies to Y1Y^{1}: after deleting one S1S_{1}-branch and shortening another one, at least two positive branches remain, so the remaining component has diameter four.

Every path of length four in UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T) has middle vertex uu, because uu is the center of the diameter-four tree UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T). Hence any copy of a component of diameter four is necessarily rooted at uu. This proves the anchoring assertion. The final assertion follows directly from the definitions: the only detached components are stars K1,tK_{1,t} with t⩾2t\geqslant 2. ∎

Because of Lemmas 4.3, 4.1, and 4.1, the inner sum over isomorphisms in the coefficient formula contributes only a non-zero constant depending on the test graph and on the rooted profile of the copy. Thus, from now on, we compute coefficients up to non-zero multiplicative constants. This is harmless, since we only use the fact that these coefficients vanish.

Branches and sub-branches.

For a vertex w∈Ssw\in S_{s}, let L⁡(w)L(w) be the set of the ss leaves adjacent with ww. The branch at ww is the subgraph

ℬ⁡(w)=T⁡[{u,w}∪L⁡(w)].\mathcal{B}(w)=T[\{u,w\}\cup L(w)].

Thus E⁡(ℬ⁡(w))={u​w}∪{w​x:x∈L⁡(w)}E(\mathcal{B}(w))=\{uw\}\cup\{wx:x\in L(w)\}, and we call ss the size of the branch. If FF is a subgraph of UG​(T)\textrm{UG}(T), the trace of FF on the branch ℬ⁡(w)\mathcal{B}(w) is

trF⁡(w)=E⁡(F)∩E⁡(ℬ⁡(w)).\operatorname{tr}_{F}(w)=E(F)\cap E(\mathcal{B}(w)).

When the copy is rooted at uu, each non-empty trace has one of the following forms.

  • •

    A central rr-sub-branch, denoted Cr​(w)C_{r}(w), consists of the central edge u​wuw together with exactly rr leaf-edges incident with ww, where 0⩽r⩽s0\leqslant r\leqslant s.

  • •

    A free rr-sub-branch, denoted Fr​(w)F_{r}(w), consists of exactly rr leaf-edges incident with ww and does not contain u​wuw, where 1⩽r⩽s1\leqslant r\leqslant s. This is a detached star K1,rK_{1,r}.

  • •

    The trace may also be empty; in that case the whole branch is absent from the chosen subgraph.

If w∈Ssw\in S_{s} and the trace is Cr​(w)C_{r}(w) with r<sr<s, we say that the branch has been shortened from ss to rr, and we write s→rs\to r. If the trace is a detached free star or is empty, we record this by an edge s→∗s\to\ast in the bookkeeping below. This notation records only the type of the copy; the actual choices of the vertices and of the retained or deleted leaves are counted in the coefficient calculation.

{lemma}

Assume p⁡(T)⩾4p(T)\geqslant 4.

  1. (i)

    Every rooted copy of ZtZ^{t}, for t=0t=0 or t⩾2t\geqslant 2, is principal: it is obtained by deleting the central edge of one branch in StS_{t}, and leaving all other branches unchanged. For t⩾2t\geqslant 2 the deleted central edge leaves a detached free tt-sub-branch; for t=0t=0 the deleted branch has empty trace.

  2. (ii)

    Let t⩾1t\geqslant 1 and let ll be odd, 1⩽l⩽t1\leqslant l\leqslant t. Every rooted copy of PltP_{l}^{t} is described by a strictly decreasing chain

    t=t0>t1>⋯>tj=t−l.t=t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{j}=t-l.

    If li=ti−ti+1l_{i}=t_{i}-t_{i+1}, then the copy is obtained by shortening one branch in StiS_{t_{i}} from tit_{i} to ti+1t_{i+1}, for each i=0,…,j−1i=0,\dots,j-1, and leaving every other branch unchanged.

  3. (iii)

    Let t⩾2t\geqslant 2 and let l⩾2l\geqslant 2 be even. Every rooted copy of QltQ_{l}^{t} is obtained as follows. First choose an anchor branch in StS_{t} and replace it by a detached free tt-sub-branch, that is, delete its central edge and keep all its leaves. Then, in the central component, choose a chain

    t=t0>t1>⋯>tj=t−lt=t_{0}>t_{1}>\cdots>t_{j}=t-l

    as in part (ii). The anchor branch is distinct from the branch of StS_{t} used at the first step of the chain.

  4. (iv)

    Every rooted copy of Y1Y^{1} has one of the following two forms. Either one branch in S1S_{1} has empty trace and a distinct branch in S1S_{1} is shortened from 11 to 00, or one branch in S0S_{0} has empty trace and two distinct branches in S1S_{1} are shortened from 11 to 00.

Proof.

By Lemma 4.3, every copy of the test graphs is rooted at the original center uu. Therefore a copy can be analyzed branch by branch using the traces defined above. We shall repeatedly use the following elementary bookkeeping fact.

Let ms=|Ss|m_{s}=|S_{s}|. Suppose that, in a rooted copy, a branch originally in SsS_{s} is shortened to a central rr-sub-branch, with r<sr<s. We record this by a directed edge s→rs\to r. Suppose also that a branch originally in SsS_{s} does not appear in the central component, either because it becomes a detached free star or because it has empty trace. We record this by a directed edge s→∗s\to\ast. Let mh′m^{\prime}_{h} be the number of central hh-sub-branches in the test graph. Then, for every level hh, we have

out⁡(h)−in⁡(h)=mh−mh′,\operatorname{out}(h)-\operatorname{in}(h)=m_{h}-m^{\prime}_{h},

where out⁡(h)\operatorname{out}(h) counts both ordinary edges h→rh\to r and edges h→∗h\to\ast, while in⁡(h)\operatorname{in}(h) counts only ordinary edges r→hr\to h. All ordinary directed edges go strictly down. Hence the finite directed multigraph formed by these edges is acyclic, and its non-trivial part decomposes into directed paths starting at the levels where mh−mh′>0m_{h}-m^{\prime}_{h}>0 and ending either at levels where mh−mh′<0m_{h}-m^{\prime}_{h}<0 or at the sink ∗\ast.

For ZtZ^{t} with t⩾2t\geqslant 2, the test graph has one detached star K1,tK_{1,t} and, in the central component, the same branch profile as TT except that one central tt-branch is missing. Thus mt−mt′=1m_{t}-m^{\prime}_{t}=1, all other differences are zero, and there is exactly one edge ending at ∗\ast. By the path decomposition above, the only possible source is level tt. The path ending at ∗\ast must therefore start at tt. It cannot contain an ordinary first step t→r<tt\to r<t, because a branch of size r<tr<t cannot contain a free tt-sub-branch. Hence this path is the single edge t→∗t\to\ast, and the copy is principal. The case t=0t=0 is the same, except that the missing branch has empty trace; since there is no ordinary edge out of level 00, all other branches are unchanged.

For PltP_{l}^{t}, the graph is connected and contains every central edge. Therefore there are no edges of the form s→∗s\to\ast. Its central profile is obtained from that of TT by replacing one central tt-branch by one central (t−l)(t-l)-branch. Hence the directed multigraph has one unit of source at tt and one unit of sink at t−lt-l. Since all ordinary edges strictly decrease the level, its non-trivial part is a single directed path

t=t0→t1→⋯→tj=t−l.t=t_{0}\to t_{1}\to\cdots\to t_{j}=t-l.

Writing li=ti−ti+1l_{i}=t_{i}-t_{i+1}, the edge ti→ti+1t_{i}\to t_{i+1} says exactly that one branch in StiS_{t_{i}} is shortened by deleting lil_{i} of its leaf-edges. This proves part (ii).

For QltQ_{l}^{t}, the graph has one detached star K1,tK_{1,t}, coming from the anchor, and its central component is obtained from the profile of TT by deleting one central tt-branch and replacing another central tt-branch by a central (t−l)(t-l)-branch. Thus the directed multigraph has two paths starting at level tt: one ending at ∗\ast, and one ending at t−lt-l. As in the case of ZtZ^{t}, the path ending at ∗\ast must be the single edge t→∗t\to\ast. This is the anchor branch. The other path is an ordinary decreasing path

t=t0→t1→⋯→tj=t−l,t=t_{0}\to t_{1}\to\cdots\to t_{j}=t-l,

which gives the chain of shortenings in the central component. These two paths start with two different outgoing edges from level tt, so they correspond to two distinct branches of StS_{t}. This proves part (iii).

Let now t⩾2t\geqslant 2, and suppose that TsT_{s} is self-converse for every s<ts<t. If St=∅S_{t}=\varnothing, there is nothing to prove. Assume St≠∅S_{t}\neq\varnothing. From cZt=0c_{Z^{t}}=0 and Lemma 4.3, we obtain

{lemma}

Let TT be an orientation of a non-path tree of diameter four, with center uu. Suppose that

For the rest of this paragraph we assume the notation of Lemma 4.3. We write

Let TT be converse invariant and let St={x,y}S_{t}=\{x,y\} be as above. Then

{lemma}

{proposition}

Let TT be a converse invariant orientation of a non-path tree of diameter four, and suppose that

∑r⩾1|Sr|=2.\sum_{r\geqslant 1}|S_{r}|=2.

Then either TT is self-converse, or the following exceptional situation holds. There is an even integer t=2​ht=2h such that

St={x,y},|S0|=t,S_{t}=\{x,y\},\qquad|S_{0}|=t,

every one of the three vertices u,x,yu,x,y has exactly hh outgoing pendant edges and exactly hh incoming pendant edges, and the two central edges are both directed away from uu, or both directed towards uu.

Proof.

Let St={x,y}S_{t}=\{x,y\}, and put s=|S0|s=|S_{0}|. By Lemma 4.3, we have

2​ou=sandox+oy=t.2o_{u}=s\qquad\text{and}\qquad o_{x}+o_{y}=t.

Assume first that the two central edges have opposite directions, say u→xu\to x and y→uy\to u. Then the branch at xx belongs to At−oxtA_{t-o_{x}}^{t}, while the branch at yy belongs to BoytB_{o_{y}}^{t}. The identity ox+oy=to_{x}+o_{y}=t is precisely

t−ox=oy.t-o_{x}=o_{y}.

Thus the two branches in StS_{t} are paired by converse. Also 2​ou=s2o_{u}=s, so the leaves in S0S_{0} are paired by converse. Hence TT is self-converse.

Consequently, if TT is not self-converse, the two central edges have the same direction, unless this is ruled out by the coefficient computation. If s≠ts\neq t, Lemma 4.3 gives ϵx+ϵy=0\epsilon_{x}+\epsilon_{y}=0, so the central edges have opposite directions, and we are back in the self-converse case. Hence every non-self-converse example must satisfy s=ts=t and must have the two central edges in the same direction. Lemma 4.3 then gives

t=2​h,ou=ox=oy=h.t=2h,\qquad o_{u}=o_{x}=o_{y}=h.

This is exactly the exceptional configuration stated above. ∎

{lemma}

The exceptional configuration of Proposition 4.3 is converse invariant.

Proof.

Let Eh+E_{h}^{+} be the exceptional tree in which the middle center is a source, and let Eh−=Eh+¯E_{h}^{-}=\overline{E_{h}^{+}} be its converse, in which the middle center is a sink. Thus Eh+E_{h}^{+} is obtained from a path

x−u−yx-u-y

by attaching 2​h2h leaves to each of x,u,yx,u,y, orienting exactly hh pendant edges away from each center and exactly hh pendant edges towards each center, and orienting the two central edges as

x←u→y.x\leftarrow u\to y.

The converse Eh−E_{h}^{-} has the same balanced pendant stars, but its central edges are oriented as

x→u←y.x\to u\leftarrow y.

It is enough to compare labeled embeddings of Eh+E_{h}^{+} and Eh−E_{h}^{-} into an arbitrary tournament TT, since Eh+E_{h}^{+} and Eh−E_{h}^{-} have the same number of automorphisms. This is the same passage from embeddings to copies used in the definition of fT​(D)f_{T}(D) in Section 2.

Fix a set C={a,b,c}C=\{a,b,c\} of three vertices of TT. We shall compare the embeddings whose three centers are mapped precisely to the vertices of CC. Call a choice of pendant leaves around CC balanced if, for each v∈Cv\in C, we choose hh vertices which receive an edge from vv and hh vertices which send an edge to vv, all these chosen vertices being distinct and lying outside CC. Such a balanced choice determines the pendant part of an embedding, up to the same leaf-labeling factor for Eh+E_{h}^{+} and Eh−E_{h}^{-}. In particular, for the comparison below, the number of balanced pendant choices depends only on TT and on CC, and not on whether we are embedding Eh+E_{h}^{+} or Eh−E_{h}^{-}.

Now consider the tournament induced by CC. There are two cases.

First suppose that T⁡[C]T[C] is cyclic. Then no vertex of CC dominates the other two vertices, and no vertex of CC is dominated by the other two vertices. Hence no vertex of CC can play the role of the middle source in Eh+E_{h}^{+}, and no vertex of CC can play the role of the middle sink in Eh−E_{h}^{-}. Therefore the set CC contributes zero embeddings of Eh+E_{h}^{+} and zero embeddings of Eh−E_{h}^{-}.

Now suppose that T⁡[C]T[C] is transitive. Let s⁡(C)s(C) be its source and let t⁡(C)t(C) be its sink. Then s⁡(C)s(C) is the unique vertex of CC which dominates the other two vertices, and t⁡(C)t(C) is the unique vertex of CC which is dominated by the other two vertices.

For an embedding of Eh+E_{h}^{+} with center set CC, the middle center uu must be mapped to s⁡(C)s(C), since uu must point to both endpoint centers. The two endpoint centers xx and yy may then be mapped to the two remaining vertices of CC in either order. Thus, after fixing the balanced pendant choices, there are exactly two possible center maps for Eh+E_{h}^{+}.

Similarly, for an embedding of Eh−E_{h}^{-} with center set CC, the middle center uu must be mapped to t⁡(C)t(C), since both endpoint centers must point towards uu. Again the two endpoint centers may be mapped to the two remaining vertices of CC in either order. Thus, after fixing the same balanced pendant choices, there are exactly two possible center maps for Eh−E_{h}^{-}.

Consequently, every transitive triple CC contributes the same number of labeled embeddings of Eh+E_{h}^{+} and Eh−E_{h}^{-}, while every cyclic triple contributes zero to both. Summing over all three-element sets C⊆V⁡(T)C\subseteq V(T) gives

embT⁡(Eh+)=embT⁡(Eh−).\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{T}(E_{h}^{+})=\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{T}(E_{h}^{-}).

Since |Aut​(Eh+)|=|Aut​(Eh−)||\text{Aut}(E_{h}^{+})|=|\text{Aut}(E_{h}^{-})|, it follows that

fT​(Eh+)=fT​(Eh−)f_{T}(E_{h}^{+})=f_{T}(E_{h}^{-})

for every tournament TT. Hence the exceptional configuration is converse invariant. ∎

{proposition}

The trees in ℰ4\mathcal{E}_{4} are converse invariant but not self-converse and cannot be obtained by the bridge-mirroring operation recursively from an orientation of a path.

Proof.

Let T∈ℰ4T\in\mathcal{E}_{4}. Then TT has

3​(2​h+1)=6​h+33(2h+1)=6h+3

vertices, which is odd. Also TT is not a path and has maximum degree 2​h+2⩾32h+2\geqslant 3.

If a tree is obtained from a path by at least one bridge-mirroring operation, then its number of vertices is even, since each bridge-mirroring step takes two disjoint copies of the previous tree and adds one bridge edge between them. Since TT is not a path, any recursive bridge-mirroring construction of TT would have to use at least one such step, and hence would produce a tree with an even number of vertices. This is impossible.

By Lemma 4.3, the tree TT is converse invariant. Moreover, TT is not self-converse: the middle vertex is the unique vertex of degree 2​h+22h+2, so every isomorphism must fix it, but reversing all arcs changes it from a source on the central path to a sink, or conversely. Therefore TT is a non-self-converse converse-invariant tree which is not obtained by recursive bridge-mirroring from a path. ∎

Putting everything together, we prove the main result of the paper:

Proof of Theorem 1.

Let TT be a converse invariant orientation of a tree of diameter four which is not a path. If

∑t⩾1|St|⩾4,\sum_{t\geqslant 1}|S_{t}|\geqslant 4,

then Theorem 4.3 implies that TT is self-converse.

It remains to consider the case

∑t⩾1|St|<4.\sum_{t\geqslant 1}|S_{t}|<4.

By Lemma 4.3, there is a unique integer t⩾1t\geqslant 1 such that St={x,y}S_{t}=\{x,y\}. Proposition 4.3 then shows that either TT is self-converse, or T∈ℰ4T\in\mathcal{E}_{4}.

Conversely, every self-converse orientation is converse invariant, and every tree in ℰ4\mathcal{E}_{4} is converse invariant by Lemma 4.3. This proves the theorem. ∎

5 A new family of non-self-converse converse invariant digraphs

It is possible to generalize the construction of Definition 1 of non-self-converse converse invariant trees using an operation we call rooted substitution. This operation provides a new way of creating converse invariant digraphs which are not self-converse. In particular, it provides counterexamples to Conjecture 1 of arbitrarily large diameter:

{definition}

Let DD be an oriented graph, and let (R,r)(R,r) be a rooted oriented graph. We write D⁡[R]D[R], the rooted substitution of RR in DD, for the oriented graph obtained as follows. For each vertex v∈V⁡(D)v\in V(D), take a copy RvR_{v} of RR, and identify the root rr of RvR_{v} with vv. The edges between the roots are the original edges of DD, and the edges inside each copy RvR_{v} are oriented as in RR.

{definition}

A rooted oriented graph (R,r)(R,r) is called rooted self-converse if there is an isomorphism

φ:R→R¯\varphi:R\to\overline{R}

such that φ⁡(r)=r\varphi(r)=r.

{proposition}

Let DD be a converse invariant oriented graph, and let (R,r)(R,r) be a rooted self-converse oriented graph. Then D⁡[R]D[R] is converse invariant. In particular, if DD and RR are trees, then D⁡[R]D[R] is a converse invariant tree.

Proof.

Let UU be an arbitrary tournament. We count labeled embeddings; this is equivalent to counting copies, since D⁡[R]D[R] and D⁡[R]¯\overline{D[R]} have the same automorphism group.

Let C⊆V⁡(U)C\subseteq V(U) be a set of size |V⁡(D)||V(D)|. We think of CC as the set of images of the vertices of DD, or equivalently, as the set of roots of the attached copies of RR. For c∈Cc\in C, let Wc⊆V⁡(U)∖CW_{c}\subseteq V(U)\setminus C be the set of vertices used for the non-root vertices of the copy of RR attached at cc. The sets WcW_{c} are required to be pairwise disjoint and to have size |V⁡(R)|−1|V(R)|-1.

For a fixed family (Wc)c∈C(W_{c})_{c\in C}, let

NU​(c,Wc)N_{U}(c,W_{c})

be the number of rooted embeddings of (R,r)(R,r) into U⁡[{c}∪Wc]U[\{c\}\cup W_{c}] which send rr to cc. Since (R,r)(R,r) is rooted self-converse, we also have

NU​(c,Wc)=NUR¯​(c,Wc),N_{U}(c,W_{c})=N_{U}^{\,\overline{R}}(c,W_{c}),

where the right-hand side denotes the number of rooted embeddings of (R¯,r)(\overline{R},r) into the same tournament, again sending the root to cc.

Define

WU​(C)=∑(Wc)c∈C∏c∈CNU​(c,Wc),W_{U}(C)=\sum_{(W_{c})_{c\in C}}\prod_{c\in C}N_{U}(c,W_{c}),

where the sum runs over all pairwise disjoint choices of the sets Wc⊆V⁡(U)∖CW_{c}\subseteq V(U)\setminus C with |Wc|=|V⁡(R)|−1|W_{c}|=|V(R)|-1. The number WU​(C)W_{U}(C) depends only on the set CC, not on any particular bijection from V⁡(D)V(D) to CC.

Now fix CC. Once the root set is CC, the choices inside the attached copies contribute the common factor WU​(C)W_{U}(C). The only remaining choice is the embedding of the base graph DD into the tournament U⁡[C]U[C]. Therefore the number of labeled embeddings of D⁡[R]D[R] into UU with root set CC is

WU​(C)​embU⁡[C]⁡(D).W_{U}(C)\,\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U[C]}(D).

Similarly, since D⁡[R]¯=D¯​[R¯]\overline{D[R]}=\overline{D}[\overline{R}] and (R,r)(R,r) is rooted self-converse, the number of labeled embeddings of D⁡[R]¯\overline{D[R]} into UU with root set CC is

WU​(C)​embU⁡[C]⁡(D¯).W_{U}(C)\,\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U[C]}(\overline{D}).

Since DD is converse invariant, we have

embU⁡[C]⁡(D)=embU⁡[C]⁡(D¯)\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U[C]}(D)=\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U[C]}(\overline{D})

for every tournament U⁡[C]U[C]. Hence the two expressions above are equal for every choice of CC. Summing over all C⊆V⁡(U)C\subseteq V(U) with |C|=|V⁡(D)||C|=|V(D)| gives

embU⁡(D⁡[R])=embU⁡(D⁡[R]¯).\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U}(D[R])=\mathop{\text{\rm emb}}\nolimits_{U}(\overline{D[R]}).

Thus D⁡[R]D[R] is converse invariant. ∎
